reference.source: Textbook of Pediatric Rheumatology / ILAR & PRINTO criteria
clinicalPearls: A rare multisystem connective tissue disease characterised by skin fibrosis together with vascular and internal organ involvement, distinguishing it from localised scleroderma
Raynaud phenomenon is usually the earliest feature and may precede skin changes by months to years, sometimes with digital ulcers or pitting scars
Skin changes progress from oedematous puffy fingers to sclerodactyly and proximal skin tightening, and nailfold capillaroscopy typically shows abnormal capillary loops
Interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension are the leading causes of mortality and require active surveillance
Gastrointestinal involvement causes reflux, dysmotility and malabsorption, while renal crisis, though rarer in children, is a hypertensive emergency
Autoantibodies such as anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) and anticentromere help characterise the disease and its organ-risk profile
Management is organ-directed and immunosuppressive, using agents such as methotrexate or mycophenolate, with vasodilators for vascular complications
reference.pathophysiology: Juvenile systemic sclerosis arises from the interplay of three processes: microvascular injury and dysfunction, immune activation with autoantibody production, and progressive fibrosis. Endothelial damage and obliterative vasculopathy underlie Raynaud phenomenon, digital ischaemia and pulmonary hypertension, while activated fibroblasts deposit excess collagen in skin and internal organs. The resulting fibrosis of lung, gut, heart and other tissues produces the characteristic multisystem morbidity. Compared with adults, children more often have overlap features and, overall, a somewhat different organ-involvement pattern.
additionalDifferentials: Mixed connective tissue disease and overlap syndromes
Scleroedema and other sclerosing skin disorders
additionalInvestigations: Antinuclear antibody with anti-Scl-70 and anticentromere antibody profiling
Nailfold capillaroscopy to detect a scleroderma pattern
Pulmonary function tests and high-resolution chest CT for interstitial lung disease
Echocardiography to screen for pulmonary arterial hypertension
Blood pressure monitoring and renal function to detect renal involvement
Gastrointestinal investigations for reflux and dysmotility when symptomatic
Skin scoring and inflammatory markers for disease monitoring
redFlags: New or worsening breathlessness suggesting interstitial lung disease or pulmonary hypertension
Accelerated hypertension with renal impairment indicating scleroderma renal crisis
Cardiac symptoms suggesting myocardial or pericardial involvement
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is determined chiefly by cardiopulmonary and renal involvement; interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension are the principal causes of death. Early detection of organ involvement and timely immunosuppressive and vasoactive therapy improve outcomes, though the disease can be chronic and disabling.
pitfalls: Dismissing isolated Raynaud phenomenon without checking for early systemic disease and abnormal capillaroscopy
Failing to screen proactively for lung and pulmonary vascular disease before symptoms appear
Confusing juvenile systemic sclerosis with localised scleroderma and underestimating organ risk
Overlooking hypertension as an early sign of renal crisis
Attributing gastrointestinal symptoms to unrelated causes
references: PRINTO/PReS/ACR-EULAR criteria for juvenile systemic sclerosis
Consensus guidance on paediatric scleroderma management
management: Immunosuppress with methotrexate or mycophenolate, escalating to cyclophosphamide or rituximab for progressive interstitial lung disease

Manage Raynaud phenomenon and digital ischaemia with calcium-channel blockers and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, adding endothelin-receptor antagonists or prostacyclin analogues for refractory digital ulcers
Treat pulmonary arterial hypertension with targeted vasodilator therapy under specialist guidance
Control gastro-oesophageal reflux and dysmotility with proton-pump inhibitors and prokinetics and address malabsorption
Treat scleroderma renal crisis as a hypertensive emergency with ACE inhibitors
Undertake active cardiopulmonary surveillance with pulmonary function tests, high-resolution CT and echocardiography
Coordinate multidisciplinary paediatric rheumatology care with physiotherapy, skin protection and specialist referral
